source.title: Understanding the Mechanism of Altruism in Large Language Models
source.authors: Shuhuai Zhang; Shu Wang; Zi-Jun Yao; Chuan-Hao Li; Xiao-Zhi Wang; Songfa Zhong; T. Liu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE feature identification and intervention to an LLM and reports results bearing on indirect evidence for recoverable SAE features. It does not reproduce or test the toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The study identifies SAE features associated with altruistic choices and intervenes on them, so those findings bear on V4. It does not measure feature overlap, neuron-level distribution, capacity pressure, or representational geometry. The neutral/generous/selfish allocation averages and generalization-game outcomes are not included as separate rows because they do not themselves measure SAE feature recovery.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained OpenSAE features on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a tool to find and manipulate features tied to Dictator Game allocations. It reports only how its own feature-selection and intervention pipeline affects behaviour. It does not measure dictionary sparsity, reconstruction quality, how features spread across neurons, polysemanticity, capacity, feature geometry or dimensionality. So it assumes rather than tests that the model contains recoverable sparse features (V4). Its results are about altruism mechanisms, not about whether superposition holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAE-identified features causally influence the model's altruistic allocations in the Dictator Game. A steering vector built from them shifts behaviour in the same direction across other social games, with negligible effects on CRT placebo questions. They caution that the features may capture only part of the process, and that the System 1/2 and semantic labels are descriptive.
record.recipe_differences: The original source concerns toy-model superposition; this study uses pretrained OpenSAE features, prompt contrasts, activation patching, and steering in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct rather than testing superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported intervention effect varies across feature groups: System 2 features have a larger reported effect than System 1 or random features, and Strategy-associated features have more effect than Sentiment-associated features. The authors also report consistency of feature selection across prompt variations and a monotonic response to steering strength.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, patching a subset of OpenSAE features chosen from a generous–selfish contrast shifts Dictator Game giving. The System 2 subset gives -10.3 pp, versus -1.0 pp for System 1 and -0.6 pp for random features. A steering vector built from these features shifts allocations in other games but has negligible effect on CRT placebo questions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features selected from a behavioural contrast can causally steer prosocial choices in an LLM. This is a steering/causal-feature result for altruism, not a measure of superposition.

record.problems: Evidence comes from one model and an SAE feature set selected using a prompted generous–selfish contrast. No uncertainty estimates are reported in the text. The authors state that they do not fully characterize feature interactions and that the identified features may represent only part of the processes producing prosocial choices.
record.rows_left_out: Figure S2 reports cosine similarity and Logit Difference Recovery by layer, but the supplied text provides no numerical values for those layer-wise traces. These figure-only per-layer measurements were not transcribed as rows; they would not establish superposition geometry in any case.

untested.parts: Toy-model overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transition and geometry; none examined.
Capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity; not examined.
Non-capacity causes of polysemanticity; not examined.
Distribution of features across neurons and sparse dictionary recoverability. The pretrained OpenSAE is assumed valid; no reconstruction, sparsity or neuron-level comparison is reported.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features. Only consistency of attribution sign across prompt variants is used, as a selection filter.
Whether features are 1-D directions. 1-D SAE directions are assumed throughout.

record.verdict_notes: Re-tranched from T3/tests to T4/uses_without_test. The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition only as background for SAEs. All rows are behavioural effects of the authors' own intervention pipeline, and none measures superposition, so the reader's V4 labels are removed. Steering generalisation (Trust Game 16.4% to 43.2%/2.8%) and the CRT placebo are not in the rows. They are also irrelevant to the versions.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transition, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity arises from capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemanticity can arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study examines SAE-recovered features in one LLM and one social-decision task; it does not test whether features are distributed across many neurons or compare SAE features with neuron-level representations.
Completeness, stability, and canonical status of SAE features.
Whether the model’s underlying features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multi-dimensional.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Selected SAE features associated with the generous–selfish representational contrast across prompt variants.

conditions.value: baseline minimal pair plus 8 validation variations

rows.measure: Number and share of candidate SAE features selected
rows.value: 2,048 candidate features; 0.024% of all SAE features across the model’s 32 layers
rows.note: The features were selected for consistent attribution to the prompted generous–selfish contrast; this is evidence of feature recovery for this contrast, not a measurement of superposition geometry.
rows.check: This is a selection value: 2,048 features kept by the authors' own attribution and consistency screen, a fixed set size. It does not measure whether a dictionary recovers the model's features.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patched the 655 identified features classified as System 1 or System 2 using activations from the contrasting persona condition.
rows.baseline: Allocation distribution under the unpatched persona prompt
rows.value: Patching reproduced nearly the full effect of patching the full 2,048-feature set
rows.note: The intervention supports a causal role for a subset of the SAE-identified features in this prompted task.
rows.check: This is a behavioural effect of patching SAE features. It tests the authors' altruism-feature hypothesis, not whether features are superposed or sparse-recoverable.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patched the remaining unclassified candidate features using activations from the contrasting persona condition.
rows.baseline: Allocation distribution under the unpatched persona prompt
rows.note: The study describes the change as small; no numeric effect size is stated.
rows.check: This compares feature subsets within the authors' own method; the paper says the change is 'only a small change'. It has no bearing on any superposition version. Marking it 'partial' for V4 was a mislink.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Replaced System 2 feature activations under the generous prompt with their selfish-condition values.
rows.baseline: Mean giving under the generous prompt before patching; numeric baseline not stated
rows.note: The reported direction is the predicted shift toward less giving.
rows.check: The shift in giving (-10.3 pp) measures the System 2 feature subset's causal role in altruism, not V4.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Replaced System 1 feature activations under the generous prompt with their selfish-condition values.
rows.baseline: Mean giving under the generous prompt before patching; numeric baseline not stated
rows.note: This was substantially smaller than the reported System 2 effect.
rows.check: The System 1 subset effect (-1.0 pp) compares the authors' own feature groups. It has no bearing on V4, so a 'partial' state is not meaningful.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patched a size-matched random set of unclassified features using selfish-condition activations.
rows.baseline: Mean giving under the generous prompt before patching; numeric baseline not stated
rows.note: This control produced a smaller change than the System 2 feature intervention.
rows.check: This is a control (random unclassified features, -0.6 pp). It serves as a baseline for R4, not as evidence on any version.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Replaced System 2 feature activations under the selfish prompt with their generous-condition values.
rows.baseline: Allocation under the selfish prompt before patching; numeric baseline not stated
rows.value: Qualitatively similar effect in the opposite direction
rows.note: The paper states that the reverse intervention increases giving in the predicted direction but gives no numeric effect size here.
rows.check: This is the reverse-direction patching effect, which the paper describes only qualitatively. It has no bearing on superposition.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patched features classified as Strategy or Sentiment using activations from the contrasting persona condition.
rows.baseline: Allocation distribution under the unpatched persona prompt
rows.note: No numeric effect size is stated in the text.
rows.check: This is the Strategy-feature patching effect (Figure S4), a comparison within the method. It is not V4 evidence.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patched features classified as Strategy or Sentiment using activations from the contrasting persona condition.
rows.baseline: Allocation distribution under the unpatched persona prompt
rows.note: The paper contrasts this with the substantial allocation changes from Strategy-feature interventions.
rows.check: This is the Sentiment-feature patching effect, which the paper says has 'little effect'. It is a comparison within the method, not V4 evidence.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: SAE-selected features were associated with the generous–selfish contrast, and patching selected feature sets shifted allocations in the predicted directions; see R1–R8.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Feature groups and controls in the Dictator Game
reader_labels.reason: Effects varied by feature group: System 1 and random-feature changes were small, unclassified features had little effect, and Sentiment-feature interventions had little effect; see R3, R5, R6, and R9.
